etymology: From the Old English mattuc, a broad-bladed hand tool for grubbing and breaking hard ground — part hoe, part pick, swung with both hands to loosen the soil, dig out roots, and clear the hillside for tillage.
biblical_def: The mattock is the labourer’s grubbing-tool, a heavy blade set crosswise on a haft and swung to break hard ground, dig out briers, and loosen the roots the plow cannot reach. Where the plow scores an open field, the mattock attacks the stubborn hillside and the thorn-choked corner by main strength of arm. Isaiah promises hills “that shall be digged with the mattock” (Isa 7:25), ground reclaimed foot by foot. Josiah carried mattocks through the cities of Manasseh and Ephraim (2Ch 34:6), breaking down the altars of the idols — the tool of tillage turned to reformation, for a land is cleared of idols as a hill is cleared of briers: by hard blows and no delicacy. But the word’s sharpest use is in the days of Saul. “Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears” (1Sa 13:19); and so “all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock” (1Sa 13:20). Israel was disarmed, and worse: for the edge of every tool they owned they must go down to their enemies and pay their enemies’ price. A covenant people who cannot sharpen their own mattock will not long hold their own field. In the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of the people — the wage of dependence, collected at the worst hour.
webster_summary: A heavy hand-tool with a broad blade, swung to grub up roots and break hard ground; part hoe, part pick.
webster_full: MATTOCK, a tool to grub up weeds or roots; a broad-bladed pick for breaking hard ground.
From the Old English mattuc; part hoe and part pick, swung with both hands.
It reclaims the stony hillside the plow cannot reach (Isa 7:25).
Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen every man his mattock (1Sa 13:20).
Josiah brake down the altars of the idols with mattocks (2Ch 34:6).

But all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock.
Isa 7:25

And so did he in the cities of Manasseh, and Ephraim, and Simeon, even unto Naphtali, with their mattocks round about.
corruption_summary: A plain farm tool, and a live parable: a people who must go down to their enemies to sharpen their own instruments have already lost the field.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a live corruption, and Israel’s mattock names it. The Philistines suffered no smith in the land, so that every man who would put an edge on his own tool must go down to his enemy and pay his enemy’s price. That is the picture of a church that borrows her instruments from the world — that takes her methods from the marketing house, her wisdom from the couch of the counsellor, her measure of success from the counting of crowds, and her courage from whatever the age will still applaud. The tool is Israel’s; the edge is the Philistine’s. And a man who must ask his enemy to sharpen his mattock will get exactly the edge his enemy wishes him to have — enough to till, never enough to fight. So it proved: in the day of battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of the people. The church that keeps no smith of her own will find, when the day of battle comes, that she has no weapon either.

The principle to recover is a forge within the camp. God has given His church her own smithy: the Scriptures, given by inspiration of God, that the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works; the preached word; prayer; the ordinances; the discipline of a true church. These are edge enough for any ground. Josiah did not borrow Philistine tools to break down the altars of the high places; he took the mattocks of Israel and swung them. Let the church sharpen her instruments at her own anvil, upon the word of the living God, and the briers of the hillside will give way — for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds.
roots_summary: The word means a broad-bladed grubbing tool for breaking hard ground and digging out roots.
roots_lines: Mattock — from the Old English mattuc, a grubbing tool.
It is part hoe and part pick, swung by the arm to break hard ground.
It digs out the roots and briers the plow cannot reach (Isa 7:25).
Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen it (1Sa 13:20).
Josiah brake down the idols’ altars with mattocks (2Ch 34:6).
usage: The mattock breaks the ground the plow refuses: some soil yields only to the blow of the arm.
Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen every man his mattock — a people disarmed at the forge.
Josiah swung mattocks against the altars: reformation is done with hard blows and no delicacy.

etymology: From the Middle English harwe, a framed implement set with iron teeth or spikes, dragged over plowed ground to break the clods and cover the seed; hence the verb, to draw such an implement, to break up and level the tilth.
biblical_def: To harrow is to drag a toothed frame across ground already plowed, breaking the clods, levelling the ridges, and covering the seed. The plow opens; the harrow breaks. It is the second labour and the unglamorous one; without it the seed lies upon lumps of unbroken earth and the field is sown to no purpose. Hosea sets the work into a prophecy: “Judah shall plow, and Jacob shall break his clods” (Hos 10:11) — the harrow’s own office, laid as a yoke upon a people who loved easier work. Ephraim was “as an heifer that is taught, and loveth to tread out the corn”: the pleasant labour, where the muzzle is free and the grain is underfoot. But the LORD passed over upon her fair neck and put her to the plow and the clods. Isaiah asks, “Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?” (Isa 28:24) — and the question answers itself: no. There is a season for breaking and a season for sowing, and the husbandman is taught of his God to know the difference. In the KJV harrows appear also as engines of war: David put the men of Rabbah “under saws, and under harrows of iron” (2Sa 12:31; 1Ch 20:3). And when the LORD would humble Job, He asked whether the wild ox would be bound in the furrow to harrow the valleys after him — the creature that takes no man’s yoke, though the God who made him rules him still.
webster_summary: An implement set with iron teeth, drawn over plowed land to break the clods and cover the seed; hence to break and level tilled ground.
webster_full: HARROW, a frame set with iron teeth, drawn over plowed ground to break the clods.
Hence the verb: to draw a harrow over; to break, level, and cover the seed.
From the Middle English harwe; the plow opens, and the harrow breaks.
The clods must be broken, or the seed lies exposed and the field is sown in vain.
Harrows of iron appear also as engines of war and judgment (2Sa 12:31).
scriptures: And Ephraim is as an heifer that is taught, and loveth to tread out the corn; but I passed over upon her fair neck: I will make Ephraim to ride; Judah shall plow, and Jacob shall break his clods.
Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?

And he brought forth the people that were therein, and put them under saws, and under harrows of iron, and under axes of iron, and made them pass through the brickkiln: and thus did he unto all the cities of the children of Ammon. So David and all the people returned unto Jerusalem.

And he brought out the people that were in it, and cut them with saws, and with harrows of iron, and with axes. Even so dealt David with all the cities of the children of Ammon. And David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the farmer’s second labour; it recovers that God breaks the clods of the heart before He sows, and that the breaking is mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a piety that wants the threshing-floor and not the furrow. Ephraim was an heifer that loved to tread out the corn — the pleasant labour, unmuzzled and well fed — and the LORD passed over upon her fair neck and put her to the plow and the clods. So the age would have a religion of pleasant work only, the harvest without the harrowing, and it names every hard providence a cruelty. But no field was ever fruitful that was not first broken. A heart all ridges and clods, however well cut with conviction, will not receive the seed until the LORD has dragged the harrow over it; and the saint who begs to be spared the teeth is begging to be left barren.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the husbandman is taught of his God. “Doth the plowman plow all day to sow? doth he open and break the clods of his ground?” No wise farmer breaks for ever; the breaking has an end, and the end is seed. So the LORD does not chide for ever, neither keepeth He His anger for ever. He wounds that He may heal, and breaks the clods of His people that the word may find soil and not stone. Let the saint under the harrow remember what the teeth are for: not to destroy the field, but to make it ready for the sowing, and after the sowing comes the sheaf.
roots_summary: The word means to drag a toothed frame over plowed ground, breaking the clods and covering the seed.
roots_lines: Harrow — Middle English harwe, a frame set with iron teeth.
It is dragged over plowed land to break the clods and cover the seed.
The plow opens the ground; the harrow breaks and levels it.
Judah shall plow, and Jacob shall break his clods (Hos 10:11).
Harrows of iron served also as engines of judgment (2Sa 12:31).
usage: The plow opens and the harrow breaks: no field is fruitful that is cut and never crumbled.
Ephraim loved to tread the corn, but the LORD put her fair neck to the plow and the clods.
The husbandman does not harrow for ever — the breaking is for the sake of the seed.

etymology: Not from the ear of corn nor the ear of the head, but from the old verb to ear — Old English erian, akin to the Latin arare, “to plow.” Earing is plowing; earing time is the season of tillage.
biblical_def: Earing in the KJV is plowing. It comes of the old verb to ear, from the same root as the Latin arare, to till and turn the ground; it has nothing whatever to do with the ear of corn or the ear of the head, and the modern reader who supposes Genesis speaks of the heading of grain has lost the whole sense. Joseph tells his brethren the famine has five years yet to run, “in the which there shall neither be earing nor harvest” (Gen 45:6): no plowing and no reaping, the year’s whole round of labour struck out at both ends, seedtime and ingathering alike suspended under the hand of God. Samuel warns Israel that the king they demand will set them “to ear his ground, and to reap his harvest” (1Sa 8:12) — the free husbandman reduced to plowing another man’s field. The elders bring the heifer down to a rough valley “which is neither eared nor sown” (Deu 21:4), ground the plow has never touched. But the word’s weight falls in the restating of the fourth commandment: “Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest: in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest” (Exo 34:21). The LORD names the two busiest hours of the farming year and commands the sabbath in both by name. Precisely where the argument for working is strongest — where the ground is ready, the weather turning, the crop standing — there the command to rest is spoken again.
webster_summary: Plowing; tillage. From the old verb “to ear,” to plow — not from the ear of corn.
webster_full: EARING, plowing; the tilling and turning of ground.
From the verb to ear, Old English erian, akin to Latin arare, “to plow.”
It has no kinship with the ear of corn nor with the ear of the head.
Earing time is the plowing season, one of the two busiest of the year.
In earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest (Exo 34:21).
scriptures: Gen 45:6
For these two years hath the famine been in the land: and yet there are five years, in the which there shall neither be earing nor harvest.
Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest: in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest.
Deu 21:4
And the elders of that city shall bring down the heifer unto a rough valley, which is neither eared nor sown, and shall strike off the heifer's neck there in the valley:

And he will appoint him captains over thousands, and captains over fifties; and will set them to ear his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war, and instruments of his chariots.
corruption_summary: The word is misread as the heading of grain; and the sabbath it guards has been surrendered to productivity, which is the deeper corruption.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live corruption here, and it is not the lexical one. The fourth commandment names earing time and harvest — the two hours of the farming year when a man could most plausibly plead necessity — and commands rest in both. Our age has learned to plead that necessity fifty-two weeks a year. Work has been promoted into the room of worship: the crowded calendar is worn as a badge of seriousness, busyness is mistaken for faithfulness, and the man who keeps the Lord’s day whole is reckoned a man who does not care whether his family eats. But the LORD who gave the harvest gave the day, and He commanded the rest at the very hour the plow was heaviest. To work through the sabbath because the season is urgent is not diligence; it is unbelief with calluses on its hands.

The principle to recover is that the sabbath is not the wage of finished work but the gift of a finishing God. Israel rested in earing time while the ground still wanted plowing, and in harvest while the grain still stood in the field, and the LORD fed them. The rest God commands does not wait upon the field being done, because the field is never done; it comes on the seventh day and calls a man off the plow whether he thinks he can spare the hour or not. That is the whole discipline of it: the rest is commanded when it costs, so that the resting is faith. He who will not lay down the mattock one day in seven has made the harvest his god, and the harvest is a hard master that never once says “enough.”
roots_summary: The word means plowing, tillage — from the old verb “to ear,” to plow.
roots_lines: Earing — from the verb to ear, Old English erian, “to plow.”
It is kin to the Latin arare, “to plow,” and not to the ear of corn.
Earing time is the plowing season, the first hard labour of the year.
Neither earing nor harvest: the famine struck out both ends of the year (Gen 45:6).
In earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest (Exo 34:21).
usage: Earing is plowing, not the heading of grain — the old verb to ear means to till.
Five years of neither earing nor harvest: the famine took the seedtime and the reaping together.
In earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest — the sabbath is commanded at the busiest hour.

etymology: From the Old French provendre, a worn form of the Latin praebenda, “that which is to be furnished, an allowance”; hence dry food for beasts — corn, meal, and the like — distinguished from straw and green fodder.
biblical_def: Provender is dry feed for cattle: grain, meal, and the mixed fodder set before an ox or an ass, distinguished from straw, which is bulk and bedding rather than nourishment. It is a small word, and Scripture uses it to mark a large virtue — the care of the beast and the completeness of a welcome. When Abraham’s servant came to Nahor’s house, “he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender for the camels, and water to wash his feet” (Gen 24:32). The camels are fed before the man eats; the beasts are part of the hospitality, and only afterward is meat set before the guest. The old man of Gibeah, pressing his roof upon the Levite, urges the same completeness: “Yet there is both straw and provender for our asses; and there is bread and wine also for me, and for thy handmaid” (Jdg 19:19). In Egypt, “as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the inn, he espied his money” (Gen 42:27) — the ordinary evening chore, and the providence of God hidden in the sack’s mouth. And Isaiah lifts the word into promise: in the day of blessing “the oxen likewise and the young asses that ear the ground shall eat clean provender, which hath been winnowed with the shovel and with the fan” (Isa 30:24). A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast, and the God who feeds the ravens has not forgotten the ass at the plow.
webster_summary: Dry food for beasts — corn, meal, and mixed fodder — distinguished from straw and green herbage.
webster_full: PROVENDER, dry food for beasts; corn, meal, and the like, given to cattle.
From the Latin praebenda, “that which is to be furnished, an allowance.”
It is distinguished from straw, which is bedding and bulk rather than feed.
Straw and provender for the camels was hospitality’s first act (Gen 24:32).
In the day of blessing the plowing oxen eat clean, winnowed provender (Isa 30:24).
scriptures: And the man came into the house: and he ungirded his camels, and gave straw and provender for the camels, and water to wash his feet, and the men's feet that were with him.
And as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the inn, he espied his money; for, behold, it was in his sack's mouth.
Yet there is both straw and provender for our asses; and there is bread and wine also for me, and for thy handmaid, and for the young man which is with thy servants: there is no want of any thing.
The oxen likewise and the young asses that ear the ground shall eat clean provender, which hath been winnowed with the shovel and with the fan.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the beast’s dry feed; it recovers a hospitality that provides down to the last ass, and a providence that reaches the manger.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a hospitality that is all table and no stable. Abraham’s servant was met with straw and provender for the camels before ever meat was set before him; the old man of Gibeah counted his welcome unfinished until the asses were fed. Our age entertains the guest it wishes to impress and forgets the beast, the servant, and the baggage — the parts of a man’s arrival that cost real trouble and win no praise. Biblical welcome is not a performance for the eye. It unloads the camels, waters the feet, and fills the manger, and it does the unseen half of the work first, before anyone is watching.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach of God’s providence. Isaiah’s promise of the good day is not of gold but of provender: the oxen and the young asses that ear the ground shall eat clean provender, winnowed with the shovel and with the fan. The plowing beast is to have the grain that has been through the winnower — a kindness so far down the order of creation that no man would have thought to promise it, and God promises it. A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast. And the Lord who counts the sparrows and clothes the grass will not fail the servant who opens his sack in the inn: what he finds there was put in by a hand that never sleeps.
roots_summary: The word means dry feed for beasts — corn and meal, as distinct from straw.
roots_lines: Provender — Old French provendre, from Latin praebenda, “an allowance.”
It denotes dry food for cattle: corn, meal, and mixed fodder.
It stands beside straw, which is bulk and bedding, not feed.
Straw and provender for the camels came before meat for the man (Gen 24:32).
The plowing beasts shall eat clean, winnowed provender (Isa 30:24).
usage: Straw and provender for the camels came before meat for the man: the welcome fed the beasts first.
He opened his sack to give his ass provender, and espied his money — providence in an evening chore.
Clean provender, winnowed with the shovel and the fan: God promises good grain to the plowing ox.

etymology: From fan, the winnowing shovel or basket, from the Latin vannus; a fanner is one who winnows — who tosses the threshed grain into the wind, that the chaff may be carried off and the wheat fall clean upon the floor.
biblical_def: A fanner is a winnower. After the threshing, the mingled heap of grain and broken husk was thrown up into the evening wind with a fan — a broad shovel or a basket — and the wind did the sorting: the heavy wheat fell back to the floor, and the light chaff blew away. Mark what the fanner does not do. He makes no difference between wheat and chaff; he only reveals the difference already there. Scripture makes the trade a figure of judgment. Against Babylon the LORD declares, “And will send unto Babylon fanners, that shall fan her, and shall empty her land” (Jer 51:2) — the Medes are His winnowing crew, and the proud city is the heap upon the floor. Against His own people He says, “And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land” (Jer 15:7). And He puts the fan into His people’s hand against their enemies: “Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away” (Isa 41:16). All of it gathers into John the Baptist’s word concerning Christ: “Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Mat 3:12). The fan is already in His hand. The floor He purges is His own — the visible church, wheat and chaff lying together in one heap through all the season, until the wind of His judgment parts them for ever.
webster_summary: Winnowers; those who toss threshed grain into the wind with a fan, that the chaff may blow away and the wheat fall clean.
webster_full: FANNER, one who fans or winnows grain; a winnower.
From fan, the winnowing shovel or basket, Latin vannus.
He throws the threshed heap into the wind; the chaff blows off, the wheat falls.
He makes no difference between wheat and chaff, but reveals it.
The LORD sends fanners unto Babylon, to fan her and empty her land (Jer 51:2).
scriptures: Jer 51:2
And will send unto Babylon fanners, that shall fan her, and shall empty her land: for in the day of trouble they shall be against her round about.
Jer 15:7
And I will fan them with a fan in the gates of the land; I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people, since they return not from their ways.
Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them: and thou shalt rejoice in the LORD, and shalt glory in the Holy One of Israel.
Mat 3:12
Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the winnower’s trade; it recovers the fan already in Christ’s hand and the parting of wheat from chaff upon His own floor.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age that has quietly retired the doctrine of judgment. Jeremiah’s fanners come to Babylon and empty her land; John says the fan is already in the hand of Christ, who will throughly purge His floor and burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire. Unquenchable: not a cleansing that ends, not a restoring that finally gathers everything into the garner, but a burning that does not go out. A pulpit that will preach the gathering of the wheat and pass over the burning of the chaff has not softened Christ’s word; it has torn the sentence in half and handed the congregation the half that costs nothing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the winnower’s plain trade, but the principle to recover is where the fanning falls. Christ purges His floor — His own threshing-floor, the visible church, where wheat and chaff have lain in one heap all the season through. The wind comes first not to Babylon but to the house of God. And mark the mercy hidden in the terror: the fan makes no chaff into wheat, and no wheat into chaff. It only discovers what every grain has been since the sowing. The elect are not made safe by the fanning; they are shown to be safe, gathered into the garner by the very wind that carries the husk away.
roots_summary: The word means winnowers — those who fan threshed grain in the wind to part the chaff from the wheat.
roots_lines: Fanner — from fan, the winnowing shovel, Latin vannus.
It denotes a winnower, one who tosses threshed grain into the wind.
The chaff is carried off; the heavy wheat falls back to the floor.
The LORD sends fanners unto Babylon, that shall fan her (Jer 51:2).
Christ’s fan is in His hand, to throughly purge His floor (Mat 3:12).
usage: I will send unto Babylon fanners — the LORD’s winnowing crew against a proud city.
The fanner makes no chaff into wheat; the wind only discovers what each grain was.
Whose fan is in his hand: Christ purges His own floor, and the chaff burns unquenchably.

etymology: From the Old English felg, the curved segment of wood or metal forming the outer rim of a wheel; several felloes, joined end to end and fixed upon the spokes, make the circle that bears upon the ground.
biblical_def: The felloes are the curved pieces that together form the outer rim of a wheel. A wheel is not turned out of one block: the nave holds the axle; the spokes radiate from it; and the felloes are jointed end to end about them into the circle that meets the road. Every felloe is an arc and nothing more — a bent piece that rolls nowhere by itself. Only in the joining is there a wheel. The word occurs once in all Scripture, in the fabric of Solomon’s temple, among the brasen bases that carried the lavers: “And the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten” (1Ki 7:33). Mark the care of the record. The Holy Ghost, having the whole glory of the house of God to describe, pauses to number the parts of a wheel on a wash-stand, and to say every one was molten — cast in the clay ground of Jordan by Hiram’s hand. Nothing in the house of God was makeshift. The bases bore the lavers in which the offerings were washed; the wheels bore the bases; the felloes bore the wheels. God’s dwelling is exact down to its rims, and He who shewed the pattern in the mount ordered the felloe too. Ezekiel’s living wheels, whose rings were dreadful and “full of eyes round about” (Eze 1:18), say the same thing: the rim is where providence touches the earth, and it sees.
webster_summary: The curved segments joined end to end to form the outer rim of a wheel; a KJV hapax, in the wheels of Solomon’s brasen bases.
webster_full: FELLOE, one of the curved pieces which, joined together, form the rim of a wheel.
From the Old English felg; the plural is felloes.
The nave holds the axle, the spokes radiate, and the felloes make the circle.
Each felloe is but an arc; only in the joining is there a wheel.
It occurs once in Scripture, a KJV hapax (1Ki 7:33).
scriptures: And the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten.
And under the borders were four wheels; and the axletrees of the wheels were joined to the base: and the height of a wheel was a cubit and half a cubit.
And every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass: and the four corners thereof had undersetters: under the laver were undersetters molten, at the side of every addition.
Eze 1:18
As for their rings, they were so high that they were dreadful; and their rings were full of eyes round about them four.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the rim of a wheel; it recovers that God’s house is exact to its smallest part, and that no member is a wheel alone.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age that despises the small and hidden work. The felloes were cast in brass for the wheels of a wash-stand — a part of a part of a vessel of the outer court, seen by few and admired by none — and God caused their making to be written in His book and kept there three thousand years. The world reckons worth by visibility and counts the unseen labour wasted. But the Lord who numbered the felloes of the lavers numbers the cup of cold water and the widow’s two mites, and no work done unto Him at the rim of the wheel is lost or forgotten.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a felloe alone is no wheel. Each is an arc — useless by itself, a bent piece of brass that will carry nothing; joined to its fellows about the spokes, it becomes a circle that bears the weight of the vessels of the house of God. So the members of Christ’s church are arcs: every one incomplete, every one shaped for a joint. The temper that prizes the untethered self would leave them scattered about the floor of the shop, each one persuaded it is round enough alone. It is not. Fitly framed together, the felloes carry the laver; scattered, they carry nothing at all.
roots_summary: The word means the curved segments which, joined together, form the outer rim of a wheel.
roots_lines: Felloe — Old English felg, the curved rim-piece of a wheel.
Several felloes, jointed end to end, make the circle of the rim.
They are fixed upon the spokes, which radiate from the nave.
A KJV hapax: the wheels of the brasen bases in Solomon’s temple (1Ki 7:33).
Axletrees, naves, felloes and spokes were all molten in brass.
usage: Naves, felloes and spokes were all molten — nothing in the house of God was makeshift.
A felloe is an arc and no more; only in the joining is there a wheel.
The Holy Ghost numbered the rim of a wash-stand’s wheel: God is exact to His smallest part.

etymology: A contraction of the Middle English engin (“engine, contrivance”), from the Latin ingenium, “a device, a piece of cunning”; hence a contrived trap — a springe or snare for taking birds and beasts. It has no kinship whatever with the distilled liquor of the same spelling.
biblical_def: A gin in the KJV is a trap: a contrived snare, sprung by a trigger, laid hidden in the path to seize a bird or a beast by the foot. The modern reader hears the name of a distilled liquor, and the two words have nothing to do with one another — the Bible’s gin is an engin, an engine, a piece of cunning set where the prey walks. Bildad, describing the end of the wicked, says “The gin shall take him by the heel, and the robber shall prevail against him” (Job 18:9). Amos makes the trap a proof of causes: “Can a bird fall in a snare upon the earth, where no gin is for him?” (Amo 3:5) — the bird does not fall by chance; something was set, and someone set it. David prays to be kept from the snares laid for him and from “the gins of the workers of iniquity” (Psa 141:9). But the word rises to doctrine in Isaiah, where the LORD Himself is the trap. He “shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Isa 8:14). One stone, and two effects. To them that trust Him, a sanctuary; to the unbelieving, a gin that takes them by the heel. Christ is not a gin because He has failed of His purpose, but because they stumble at Him, “whereunto also they were appointed” (1Pe 2:8).
webster_summary: A contrived trap or snare for taking birds and beasts; from engin, an engine — not the distilled liquor of the same spelling.

corruption_summary: The word is misheard as the liquor; and the doctrine it carries — that the same Christ is sanctuary to the elect and gin to the unbelieving — is the offence the age will not have.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a live corruption, and it is not chiefly the drink. Isaiah says the LORD of hosts Himself shall be “for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” — and Paul and Peter both take up that stone and lay it upon Christ: “Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence” (Rom 9:33; 1Pe 2:8). One stone, two effects, and God ordains both. The age insists that Christ is offered evenhandedly and that the whole difference lies in the will of the man; but Peter writes of them that stumble at the word, being disobedient, “whereunto also they were appointed.” The stumbling is not an accident of the gospel or a failure of its aim. It is the purpose of God, who hides these things from the wise and prudent and reveals them unto babes; and it is not for the clay to answer back to Him that formed it.

The mercy is in the other half of the same verse. The stone that is a gin to the inhabitants of Jerusalem is a sanctuary to the houses that trust Him — and He is a sanctuary effectually, not conditionally. Christ did not lay down His life to make salvation possible for all and certain for none; He laid it down for His sheep, and His sheep hear His voice and are not snared. Amos asks whether a bird falls in a snare where no gin is for him: nothing falls by chance, and neither does anything stand by chance. The elect are kept from the gins of the workers of iniquity by the same sovereign hand that appointed the stumbling of the disobedient. Every soul that trusts the stone finds it a sanctuary, for whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.

etymology: From the Latin puls, “a thick pottage of meal or beans”; hence the edible seeds of leguminous plants — beans, lentiles, peas — and the plain food made of them. It is wholly distinct from the pulse of the blood, which comes of the Latin pellere, “to beat.”
biblical_def: Pulse is the leguminous seed-food of the ancient table — beans, lentiles, peas — and the plain pottage made from them. The modern reader hears the beating of the blood at the wrist; but that pulse is a different word altogether, from the Latin pellere, to beat, while the Bible’s pulse is from puls, a thick pottage of meal and beans. It is peasant fare. Among the provisions Barzillai and his fellows carried out to David in his flight were “wheat, and barley, and flour, and parched corn, and beans, and lentiles, and parched pulse” (2Sa 17:28): the simple stores of the countryside, brought to a hunted king. The word’s great hour is in Babylon. “Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king’s meat, nor with the wine which he drank” (Dan 1:8), and he said to the steward, “Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink” (Dan 1:12). At the end of ten days their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children who did eat the portion of the king’s meat, and so “Melzar took away the portion of their meat, and the wine that they should drink; and gave them pulse” (Dan 1:16). The issue was never the beans. It was a young captive’s refusal to be defiled at a pagan king’s table, and a God who honoured him for it.

corruption_summary: A live and commercial corruption: the “Daniel Diet” trade has turned a chapter about covenant faithfulness under a pagan king into a programme for the body.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a live corruption with a price tag upon it. Daniel 1 has been mined for a “Daniel Diet” and a “Daniel Fast” — books, meal plans, twenty-one-day challenges, branded supplements — upon the claim that Scripture is here recommending a regimen. It is not. Daniel did not eat pulse because pulse is nourishing; he ate pulse because the king’s meat was defiled, and he had purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself. Strip the covenant out of the chapter and what is left is a health tip with a prophet’s name on the label. That is the corruption: a boy’s holy refusal in a hostile court, sold back to the church as a way to feel better and lighter. The text is about a table, and the table is about a throne — whose servant Daniel would be.

The principle to recover is that God gave the increase. God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs (Dan 1:9); God made the countenances fair; God gave the four children knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom (Dan 1:17). Ten days of beans and water do not by any arithmetic of nature make a captive fairer and fatter in flesh than a court fed on the king’s own meat. The result was a miracle and not a menu, and it was wrought to vindicate a young man who risked his place and perhaps his neck rather than be defiled. Do not take the recipe and leave the resolve. What Scripture commends here is no diet but a purpose of heart — the settled determination, in a pagan court and at real cost, to refuse the defilement and leave the consequences with God.

etymology: From the Old French teil, til, from the Latin tilia, “the linden or lime tree”; the KJV’s name for a great spreading tree of Palestine (the terebinth) which, stripped or felled, keeps its life in the stock and sprouts again.
biblical_def: The teil tree is the KJV’s name for a great tree of the land — the terebinth, set by the translators beside the oak — and it is called teil from the Latin tilia, the linden. It appears once, and carries one of the weightiest doctrines of the prophets. Isaiah is sent to preach to a people who will not hear, until the cities be wasted without inhabitant and the LORD have removed men far away (Isa 6:12). Then comes the exception: “But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof” (Isa 6:13). Here is the remnant. The teil and the oak cast their leaves and stand bare through the winter as though dead — but the substance is in them. Cut such a tree to the ground and the stock lives; the sap holds in the stump, and it sprouts again. So Israel is felled to a tenth, and the tenth is eaten down again, and still the holy seed is the substance thereof. God never leaves Himself without a stump. Out of that very stock came the rod out of the stem of Jesse (Isa 11:1); and Christ is the true holy Seed in whom the remnant stands, for “even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5).

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the name of a tree; it recovers the remnant — the stump whose substance lives, the holy seed, and Christ the rod out of the stem.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes both the despair and the presumption of the age. Isaiah’s commission is the bleakest in the prophets — preach until the cities be wasted without inhabitant and the houses without man — and a church that reads the times and concludes God has finished with His people has read only to the end of the twelfth verse. But neither may any man presume upon the tenth. The tenth itself “shall return, and shall be eaten”: the remnant is winnowed and winnowed again, and mere descent from Abraham saves nobody. Judgment falls upon the tree, and falls again upon what is left of the tree, and what stands at the last stands by election and not by pedigree.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of the remnant, and it is written in the wood. The teil tree and the oak cast their leaves and stand all winter like dead things — but “whose substance is in them.” The sap is in the stock; cut the trunk to the ground and the stump lives and sprouts. So God has never left Himself without witness: seven thousand who bowed not the knee to Baal, a tenth in Isaiah’s ruin, “a remnant according to the election of grace.” And the stump is not the end of the story but the beginning of it — out of the stem of Jesse came forth the rod, and Christ is Himself the holy Seed that is the substance of the whole. Where the world sees a felled tree, God sees His Son and His elect in Him.

etymology: From boll, the rounded seed-pod or capsule of a plant (Old English bolla, “a bowl, a rounded vessel”); hence bolled, “podded, gone to seed-vessel” — the flax standing in bud, and so near to its ripening.
biblical_def: Bolled means podded — formed into the boll, the rounded seed-vessel of the flax, as a bowl is a rounded thing; the two words are one. To say the flax was bolled is to say it stood in bud, its capsules formed, within a few weeks of harvest. The word occurs once in all Scripture, and it occurs as a date: “And the flax and the barley was smitten: for the barley was in the ear, and the flax was bolled” (Exo 9:31). The seventh plague fell upon a growing field, and Moses tells us exactly what stage the crops had reached — barley in the ear, flax in the boll — and then tells us what the hail spared: “But the wheat and the rie were not smitten: for they were not grown up” (Exo 9:32). Barley and flax head early; wheat and spelt head late. That is a particular few weeks of the Egyptian year, and the record is precise enough to be laid against the growing season of the Nile. The Holy Ghost did not have to say this. He said it because the plagues were not a parable but an event — in a real month, on a real crop, in a real country — and the hail smote “throughout all the land of Egypt all that was in the field” (Exo 9:25), while “only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, was there no hail” (Exo 9:26). The judgment was datable, and the mercy was addressed.
webster_summary: Podded; formed into the boll, the rounded seed-vessel — said of the flax standing in bud, near its ripening.

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but an old word for podded; it recovers that the plagues fell upon a datable harvest — history, and not parable.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the habit of reading the Exodus as a story about God rather than an account of what God did. One participle fixes the calendar: the flax was bolled and the barley was in the ear, while the wheat and the rie were not grown up. Barley and flax head early in Egypt, and wheat and spelt head late; that is a particular few weeks of a particular year, and Moses states it because he was there and saw it. Scripture does not date a fable. The hail fell upon a field a man could have walked out into and counted the broken stalks, and the God who sent it acts in months and mornings, not in edifying ideas.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself, and the plague it dates is plain history. The principle to recover is that the judgment was addressed. The hail smote throughout all the land of Egypt all that was in the field, both man and beast, and brake every tree of the field — and “only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, was there no hail.” The same storm that ruined the flax of Egypt did not bruise a boll in Goshen. The wrath of God is not weather: it falls where He sends it and it stops where He says. The bolled flax of Egypt and the untouched flax of Goshen, under one sky in one hour, preach the discriminating mercy that shelters His own in the day of His anger.
